claim: Eight male Long-Evans rats (3–6 months, 450–650 g) were used for experiments.
source: Eight male Long-Evans rats (3–6 months, 450–650 g, RRID: RGD_2308852) were used for experiments.
evidence: Directly stated in the Methods section describing the animals used.

claim: Animals maintained a high level of performance on the task during electrophysiological recording (77.0% ± 1.3%, mean ± s.e.m.).
source: Following post-operative recovery and during electrophysiological recording, animals maintained a high level of performance on the task, indicating accurate decision making based on cued recall of odor-place associations (Figure 1b, n=8 rats, 77.0% ± 1.3%, mean ± s.e.m.).
evidence: Quantitative performance data from 8 rats during recording sessions.

claim: The average odor-sampling duration before odor port disengagement and odor offset was 0.82±0.02 s (mean ± s.e.m. across sessions).
source: The average odor-sampling duration before odor port disengagement and odor offset was 0.82±0.02 s (mean ± s.e.m. across sessions), and this duration was similar between correct and incorrect trials (Figure 1c; within-session signed-rank test, p=0.71, distribution for all trials shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Measured behavioral data across recording sessions.

claim: Odor sampling duration was similar between correct and incorrect trials (p=0.71).
source: The average odor-sampling duration before odor port disengagement and odor offset was 0.82±0.02 s (mean ± s.e.m. across sessions), and this duration was similar between correct and incorrect trials (Figure 1c; within-session signed-rank test, p=0.71, distribution for all trials shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Statistical comparison using signed-rank test.

claim: There was a small but significant increase in sniff rate during the odor sampling period (7.1±0.39 Hz) compared to time matched pre-odor periods (6.2±0.29 Hz).
source: There was a small but significant increase in sniff rate during the odor sampling period (within-session increase 7.1±0.39 Hz, mean ± s.e.m.) compared to time matched pre-odor periods (6.2±0.29 Hz, mean ± s.e.m.) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: Thermocouple measurements of sniff rate in two animals.

claim: On 95.4% ± 0.12% of trials, the animals' turn direction away from the odor port matched the direction of the T-maze reward arm that they would ultimately choose.
source: Notably, we observed that on a majority of trials (95.4% ± 0.12%), the animals' turn direction away from the odor port matched the direction of the T-maze reward arm that they would ultimately choose on that trial.
evidence: Behavioral observation across trials.

claim: The turn direction matching occurred regardless of whether the trial was correct or incorrect (correct trials: p=0; incorrect trials: p=1.4e-108).
source: This behavioral phenomenon was not required for successful performance of the task, and it occurred regardless of whether the trial was correct or incorrect (Figure 1d; within-session binomial tests, correct trials: p=0; incorrect trials: p=1.4e-108).
evidence: Statistical analysis using binomial tests on behavioral data.

claim: Beta band (20–30 Hz) power increased during the decision-making period compared to a time-matched pre-odor period across all three regions (CA1 P=2.84e-3, PFC P=1.80e-4, OB P=8.3e-6).
source: We observed a strong increase in power in the beta band (20–30 Hz) during this decision-making period compared to a time-matched pre-odor period across all three regions (Figure 2b and d, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, n=38 sessions, CA1 P=2.84e-3, PFC P=1.80e-4, OB P=8.3e-6).
evidence: Statistical analysis of LFP power across 38 sessions.

claim: The respiratory rhythm (RR, 7–8 Hz) was prominent in the LFP in all three regions but did not increase significantly following odor onset.
source: The respiratory rhythm (RR, 7–8 Hz) was also prominent in the LFP in all three regions but did not increase significantly following odor onset (Figure 2d).
evidence: LFP analysis showing presence but no significant increase.

claim: Beta coherence between CA1-PFC, CA1-OB, and PFC-OB significantly increased from pre-odor to odor-sampling period (CA1-PFC p=2.8e-3, CA1-OB p=5.1e-5, PFC-OB p=3.7e-5).
source: This coherence was specific to the odor-sampling period: it significantly increased compared to time-matched pre-odor periods (Figure 2e top, signed-rank test, n=38 sessions, CA1-PFC p=2.8e-3, CA1-OB p=5.1e-5, PFC-OB p=3.7e-5), and diminished shortly after the rat exited the odor port, once the decision had been made (Figure 2c).
evidence: Statistical analysis of coherence across 38 sessions.

claim: RR coherence increased from the pre-odor to the odor-sampling period for all region pairs (CA1-OB p=6.4e-4, CA1-PFC p=3.9e-3, PFC-OB p=2.4e-4).
source: Network wide coherence in the RR band also increased from the pre-odor to the odor-sampling period (Figure 2e top, signed-rank test, CA1-OB p=6.4e-4, CA1-PFC p=3.9e-3, PFC-OB p=2.4e-4).
evidence: Statistical analysis of RR coherence.

claim: Beta coherence during the decision-making period was significantly higher than coherence at the reward well between all three region pairs (CA1-PFC p=0.010, CA1-OB p=0.0012, PFC-OB p=0.0024).
source: We confirmed that beta coherence observed during the decision-making period was significantly higher than coherence at the reward well between all three pairs (Figure 2e middle, signed-rank test, CA1-PFC p=0.010, CA1-OB p=0.0012, PFC-OB p=0.0024).
evidence: Statistical comparison between task epochs.

claim: Beta coherence was significantly lower in air-only sessions compared to odor-cued sessions.
source: RR coherence was unchanged between odor- and air-cued sessions, but beta coherence was significantly lower in the absence of odor cues during air-only sessions (Figure 2g).
evidence: Comparison between odor-cued and air-only control sessions.

claim: SWR events occurred frequently at the two reward locations but were rare at the odor port (p=1.1e-7).
source: SWR events occurred frequently at the two reward locations, as expected (Buzsáki et al., 1983). However, a distinct lack of SWR events at the odor port (Figure 2f; signed-rank test, p=1.1e-7) suggests that SWR replay is unlikely to play a direct role in decision making based on recalled associative memories for this well-learned task.
evidence: Statistical comparison of SWR occurrence across task locations.

claim: There was no significant change in beta or RR coherence or power between correct and incorrect trials.
source: There was no significant change in the level of coherence or power in the CA1-PFC-OB network in either frequency band between correct and incorrect trials (Figure 2e bottom, signed-rank tests; all p's>0.05).
evidence: Statistical comparison between correct and incorrect trials.

claim: 1,309 units were recorded from hippocampal area CA1 and 717 units from PFC.
source: In addition to LFP, we assessed neuronal activity in the task by recording single units from hippocampal area CA1 (n=1,309 units) and PFC (n=717 units) (distribution of neurons across animals shown in table in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Direct count of recorded units.

claim: 934 CA1 units and 508 PFC units fired at least 100 spikes during the run epochs.
source: Therefore we first selected units that fired at least 100 spikes during the run epochs (Figure 3g–h, 'Active Cells', 934 in CA1, 508 in PFC) and categorized them into pyramidal cells and interneurons based on firing rate and spike width (see Methods, CA1: 813 (87%) pyramidal, 121, (13%) interneurons; PFC: 464 (91%) pyramidal, 44 (9%) interneurons).
evidence: Classification of recorded units based on activity criteria.

claim: 170 CA1 cells (21%) and 234 PFC cells (50%) were active during the odor period.
source: For analyses during the decision-making period, we then selected for cells that were active during the odor period with the criterion that they fired at least as many spikes as there were trials ('Odor Period Active', see Methods, CA1: 170/813,21% PFC: 234/464, 50%).
evidence: Classification based on odor period activity criteria.

claim: 81% of odor-active CA1 cells and 79% of odor-active PFC cells were task-responsive.
source: The majority of these active cells were also task responsive and exhibited significant changes in firing rate following the onset of odor sampling (see Methods and Figure 3g–h; n=138/170, 81% task-responsive CA1 cells, n=185/234, 79%, task-responsive PFC cells).
evidence: Statistical classification of task-responsive cells.

claim: 34% of task-responsive CA1 pyramidal cells and 31% of task-responsive PFC pyramidal cells were choice-selective.
source: To determine significance, the SI value for each task responsive pyramidal cell was compared to a distribution of SIs generated by shuffling the odor identities across trials (n=47/138, 34% CA1 selective cells, n=59/185, 31% PFC selective cells) (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Statistical determination of choice selectivity.

claim: Selectivity indices on correct trials were anti-correlated with selectivity indices on incorrect trials for CA1 pyramidal cells (r=–0.58, p=1.82e-5).
source: We found that this phenomenon held true across the population of selective pyramidal cells, such that overall, the SIs on correct trials were anti-correlated with the SIs on incorrect trials (Figure 3e–f for tuning curves locked to odor onset (left) and offset (right) on correct (top) and incorrect (bottom) trials, and also Figure 3i and j for selectivity scores during correct versus incorrect trials, Spearman Rank Correlation, CA1 pyr correct-incorrect SI r=–0.58, p(47) = 1.82e-5, PFC pyr correct-incorrect SI r=–0.68, p(59) = 3.47e-9).
evidence: Statistical correlation analysis of selectivity indices.

claim: Selectivity indices on correct trials were anti-correlated with selectivity indices on incorrect trials for PFC pyramidal cells (r=–0.68, p=3.47e-9).
source: We found that this phenomenon held true across the population of selective pyramidal cells, such that overall, the SIs on correct trials were anti-correlated with the SIs on incorrect trials (Figure 3e–f for tuning curves locked to odor onset (left) and offset (right) on correct (top) and incorrect (bottom) trials, and also Figure 3i and j for selectivity scores during correct versus incorrect trials, Spearman Rank Correlation, CA1 pyr correct-incorrect SI r=–0.58, p(47) = 1.82e-5, PFC pyr correct-incorrect SI r=–0.68, p(59) = 3.47e-9).
evidence: Statistical correlation analysis of selectivity indices.

claim: CA1 interneurons showed anti-correlation in selectivity between correct and incorrect trials (r=–0.80, p=3.4e-8).
source: For CA1 interneurons, the selectivity response showed anti-correlation during correct versus incorrect trials similar to that of pyramidal cells (Figure 4c top, r(32) = –0.80, p=3.4e-8) suggesting coordination between these cell populations as well as a functional role in the decision making period.
evidence: Statistical correlation analysis for interneurons.

claim: PFC interneurons' selectivity indices on correct and incorrect trials were not anti-correlated (r=–0.38, p=0.278).
source: PFC interneurons' SIs on correct and incorrect trials were not anti-correlated, although this could result from the overall low number of selective PFC interneurons (Figure 4c bottom r(10) = –0.38, p=0.278).
evidence: Statistical correlation analysis for PFC interneurons.

claim: CA1-PFC interneuron pairs showed significant temporal coordination with PFC interneurons leading (p=3.5e-8).
source: We found a significant skew in CA1-PFC interneuron pairs towards the PFC interneurons leading (sign rank test, x=–0.028, p=3.5e-8) (Figure 4d), as well as for CA1 pyramidal cell - PFC interneuron pairs in the same direction (sign rank test, x=–0.013, p=0.0034).
evidence: Cross-correlation analysis of spike timing between regions.

claim: 82% of task-responsive CA1 pyramidal cells and 89% of CA1 interneurons were significantly locked to the local RR.
source: A large subset of cells within the population of task-responsive cells in CA1 (Figure 5c, CA1 Pyr locked to local RR n=113/138, 82%, interneurons to local RR n=74/83, 89%) and a smaller population of cells in PFC were significantly locked to the local RR (Figure 5c, PFC Pyr to local RR n=42/185, 23%, PFC interneurons to local RR n=12/28, 43%).
evidence: Phase-locking analysis using Rayleigh Z test.

claim: 20% of CA1 pyramidal cells and 43% of CA1 interneurons were coherent to local beta.
source: Surprisingly though, while a modest but significant proportion of CA1 pyramidal cells were also coherent to local beta (28/138, 20% binomial test p=4.6e-11) a large fraction of CA1 interneurons were coherent to local beta (36/83, 43%).
evidence: Phase-locking analysis with statistical significance testing.

claim: 11% of CA1 interneurons were significantly locked to PFC beta (p=1.7e-20).
source: When we assessed cross-regional spike-beta coherence, we found that there were significantly more CA1 interneurons locked to PFC beta than chance (Figure 5c–d, Binomial test on significantly (Bonferonni adjusted alpha = 0.0167) coherent proportion, see Methods; CA1 interneurons coherent maximally to PFC beta n=9/83 11%, p=1.7e-20 to OB beta 2/138 1.5% p=0.2), but no high degree of cross regional spike-phase coherence for CA1 Pyramidal cells (CA1 pyr coherent maximally to PFC beta n=11/138, 8.0%, to OB beta 10/138, 7.3%, all p>0.0167) or for PFC cells (Figure 5c–d, PFC: pyr maximally coherent to CA1 beta n=10/185, 5.4%, to OB beta n=3/138, 2.2% PFC interneurons maximally coherent to CA1 beta n=3/28 10.7%, to OB beta n=0/28 0%, all p>0.0167).
evidence: Cross-regional phase-locking analysis with statistical testing.

claim: Beta-locked CA1 pyramidal cells, CA1 interneurons, and PFC pyramidal cells exhibited lower mean vector length on incorrect trials compared to correct trials (CA1 pyr p=0.014, CA1 IN p=0.038, PFC pyr p=0.039).
source: We found that both pyramidal cells and interneurons in CA1 and pyramidal cells in PFC that were phase-locked to the local beta rhythm exhibited a lower MVL on incorrect trials (Figure 5e, signed-rank tests, CA1: pyr n=28, p=0.014, IN n=36, p=0.038; PFC: pyr n=8, p=0.039, in n=2, these few interneurons did show a decrease).
evidence: Statistical comparison of phase-locking strength between correct and incorrect trials.

claim: There was no significant effect of RR phase locking on trial accuracy.
source: There was no significant effect for local RR phase locking (Figure 5f, signed-rank test, no significance found).
evidence: Statistical comparison showing no significant difference.

claim: CA1 interneurons showed decreased cross-region spike-phase coherence to PFC beta on incorrect trials (p=0.0023).
source: Interestingly, cross-region spike-phase coherence showed a similar relationship to decision accuracy for CA1 phase-coherent interneurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 2 n=20, p=0.0023) suggesting a central role for CA1 interneurons in synchronizing PFC-CA1 activity and enabling a correct choice.
evidence: Statistical analysis of cross-regional coherence related to accuracy.

claim: Neural discrimination times for CA1 and PFC during odor sampling were similar (p=0.68).
source: Neural discrimination times for CA1 and PFC (n=24 sessions across 8 animals; threshold of 4 task-responsive cells, CA1: 200–800ms; PFC: 400–700ms) were similar (Figure 6d; p=0.68, sign-rank test).
evidence: Statistical comparison of neural discrimination timing between regions.

claim: Reward choice could be accurately predicted 0.1 s prior to odor port disengagement by CA1 ensembles using task-responsive pyramidal cells.
source: When we performed this analysis using task-responsive putative pyramidal cells we found that reward choice could be accurately predicted 0.1 s prior to odor port disengagement by CA1 ensembles, and 0.3 s prior by PFC ensembles (Figure 6e left).
evidence: GLM prediction analysis of ensemble activity.

claim: Reward choice could be accurately predicted 0.3 s prior to odor port disengagement by PFC ensembles using task-responsive pyramidal cells.
source: When we performed this analysis using task-responsive putative pyramidal cells we found that reward choice could be accurately predicted 0.1 s prior to odor port disengagement by CA1 ensembles, and 0.3 s prior by PFC ensembles (Figure 6e left).
evidence: GLM prediction analysis of ensemble activity.

claim: Including interneurons improved CA1 ensemble prediction to 0.2 s prior to decision execution.
source: We also performed the same analysis but after included both task-responsive pyramidal and interneurons in the ensembles (Figure 6e right). In this case, we found an improvement in prediction for CA1 ensembles: reward prediction was now accurate starting earlier, at 0.2 s prior to decision execution.
evidence: GLM prediction analysis comparing different cell populations.

claim: 344 out of 585 CA1 cells and 159 out of 288 PFC cells had spatial fields on the track.
source: A large fraction of cells in CA1 and PFC exhibited spatial activity on the maze (see Methods for details on spatial parameters, n=344 out of 585 CA1 cells; n=159 out of 288 PFC cells had fields on the track), including units that were both active during the odor period (choice selective and non-selective) and inactive during these periods (Figure 7a and b; examples of CA1 and PFC choice-selective cells with spatial fields in Figure 7a, examples of CA1 and PFC odor active but non-selective cells with spatial fields shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Spatial field analysis of recorded units.

claim: Odor period active cells were more likely to have spatial fields on the track compared to inactive cells (CA1: p=0.029; PFC: p=2.7e-5).
source: Cells that were odor period active were more likely to have spatial fields on the track (odor sampling periods were excluded in spatial responses, see Methods), compared to cells that were not (Figure 7b, binomial test, CA1: p=0.029; PFC: p=2.7e-5).
evidence: Statistical comparison of spatial field prevalence.

claim: There was no difference in spatial field width between odor period active and inactive cells (CA1: p=0.15; PFC: p=0.92).
source: Surprisingly however, we found no difference in field width (Figure 7c, rank-sum tests, CA1: p=0.15; PFC: p=0.92), field peak rate (Figure 7—figure supplement 1c), or field sparsity (Figure 7—figure supplement 1d) between cells that were odor period active or inactive in either region.
evidence: Statistical comparison of spatial field characteristics.

claim: There was no relationship between preferred trajectory during run periods and preferred choice during the odor-cued decision-making period (CA1: p=0.26; PFC: p=0.20).
source: Interestingly, although trajectory-selective cells were significantly more likely than trajectory-nonselective cells to respond in the decision-making period (Figure 7—figure supplement 1e), there was no relationship between the preferred trajectory during run periods and preferred choice during the odor-cued decision-making period (Figure 7d, rank sum test CA1: p=0.26; PFC: p=0.20).
evidence: Statistical comparison of trajectory and choice selectivity.

claim: Choice identity could be decoded at the first quintile of track nearest to the odor port, but decoding accuracy diminished to chance level thereafter.
source: We found that choice identity could be decoded at the first quintile of track, nearest to the odor port, but decoding accuracy diminished to chance level thereafter (Figure 7e).
evidence: Bayesian decoder analysis of ensemble activity across spatial locations.

claim: The animal's upcoming behavioral choice could be accurately decoded at all periods along the trajectory using spatially active ensembles in each respective spatial quintile.
source: In contrast, the animal's upcoming behavioral choice could be accurately decoded at all periods along the trajectory if instead the spatially active ensembles in each respective spatial quintile was used as the training set (Figure 7f).
evidence: Bayesian decoder analysis using spatially-modulated ensembles.

claim: Beta and RR rhythms govern physiological coordination between the olfactory bulb, hippocampus, and PFC during odor-place associative memory task.
source: We found that during an odor-place associative memory task, beta and RR rhythms govern physiological coordination between the olfactory bulb, hippocampus, and PFC (OB-CA1--PFC).
evidence: Summary of findings from LFP coherence analyses.

claim: CA1-PFC beta coordination during the decision-making period is linked to decision accuracy.
source: Crucially, CA1-PFC beta coordination during the decision-making period of this task is linked to decision accuracy.
evidence: Summary of findings relating beta coherence to performance.

claim: Task-responsive single unit and ensemble activity in the CA1-PFC network discriminates between choices and can reliably predict upcoming behavior during the odor sampling and decision-making period.
source: During the odor sampling and decision-making period, task-responsive single unit and ensemble activity in the CA1-PFC network discriminates between choices and can reliably predict upcoming behavior.
evidence: Summary of single unit and ensemble analyses.

claim: Different cell ensembles were engaged in CA1-PFC during decision-making vs. decision execution on the maze.
source: Different cell ensembles were engaged in CA1-PFC during decision-making vs. decision execution on the maze.
evidence: Summary of spatial decoding analyses showing distinct ensembles.

claim: Rhythmic coordination within the hippocampal-prefrontal-olfactory bulb network supports utilization of odor cues for memory-guided decision making.
source: Our findings indicate that rhythmic coordination within the hippocampal-prefrontal-olfactory bulb network supports utilization of odor cues for memory-guided decision making.
evidence: Overall conclusion synthesizing multiple findings.

claim: Rats were required to hold their nose in the odor port for a minimum of 0.50 s on each trial.
source: Rats were required to hold their nose in the odor port for a minimum of 0.50 s on each trial, but could continue sniffing the odor for any length of time after the minimum threshold was reached.
evidence: Description of task requirements.

claim: The odor was continuously dispensed for the entire duration of time that the rat held its nose in the odor port.
source: The odor was continuously dispensed for the entire duration of time that the rat held its nose in the odor port and was only turned off once the rat disengaged from the odor-port.
evidence: Description of odor delivery protocol.

claim: The animals' average velocity during the task showed a decrease in speed from the pre-odor period to the odor sampling period.
source: The animals' average velocity during the task showed a decrease in speed from the pre-odor period to the odor sampling period in the odor port, followed by an increase in speed after they left the odor port to run to the reward location (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b–c).
evidence: Behavioral velocity measurements across task epochs.

claim: Rapid movement away from the odor-port was observed after odor-port disengagement.
source: We observed rapid movement away from the odor-port after odor-port disengagement (Figure 1—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: Behavioral observation of movement patterns.

claim: The time of disengagement from the odor port provides a trial-by-trial estimate of the moment at which the animal executes the decision.
source: The time of disengagement from the odor port thus provides a trial-by-trial estimate of the moment at which the animal executes the decision.
evidence: Inference based on behavioral observation that turn direction matches ultimate choice.

claim: The odor sampling period corresponds to odor-cued recall of the learned association and priming of the subsequent decision to turn toward the reward location.
source: The odor sampling period thus corresponds to odor-cued recall of the learned association and priming of the subsequent decision to turn toward the reward location, with a behavioral report of the decision occurring at odor port offset.
evidence: Interpretation based on behavioral observations.

claim: Phase-amplitude coupling was observed between RR and beta rhythms in all three regions.
source: During the decision-making period, we also found phase-amplitude coupling between beta and RR rhythms in all three regions, consistent with previous findings (Lockmann et al., 2016; Figure 2—figure supplement 1f), and suggesting a mechanistic relationship between the two rhythms.
evidence: Phase-amplitude coupling analysis with citation to previous work.

claim: The beta rhythm is not merely a harmonic of RR.
source: Despite this relationship, previous literature shows that the two rhythms are differentially generated and maintained in the olfactory system and hippocampus and appear to serve different functions in olfactory processing (Kay, 2014; Kay et al., 2009; Martin et al., 2006; Neville and Haberly, 2003), indicating that the beta rhythm is not merely a harmonic of RR.
evidence: Interpretation based on cited literature and observed power differences.

claim: CA1-PFC beta coherence was elevated during the decision-making period but did not differ between correct vs. incorrect trials.
source: CA1-PFC-OB beta coherence was elevated during the decision-making period, but we did not find evidence for difference in coherence for correct vs. incorrect trials.
evidence: Summary of coherence analysis results.

claim: A CA1-PFC sub-population of phase-locked cells exhibited stronger phase modulation by beta rhythms on correct vs. incorrect trials.
source: Instead, we found that a CA1-PFC sub-population of phase-locked cells exhibited stronger phase modulation by beta rhythms on correct vs. incorrect trials.
evidence: Summary of phase-locking analysis results.

claim: CA1 interneurons exhibited cross-regional spike-phase beta coherence and higher phase modulation to PFC beta during correct trials.
source: CA1 interneurons exhibited cross-regional spike-phase beta coherence and higher phase modulation to PFC beta during correct trials, and showed temporal coordination with PFC neurons in cross-correlations.
evidence: Summary of interneuron-specific analyses.

claim: Coordination by odor-driven beta rhythms can sculpt network activity through interneuron modulation, enabling emergence of task-related ensemble dynamics in local circuits to support decision making.
source: This suggests that coordination by odor-driven beta rhythms can sculpt network activity through interneuron modulation, enabling emergence of task-related ensemble dynamics in local circuits to support decision making.
evidence: Interpretation synthesizing multiple findings about interneurons and beta rhythms.

claim: Oscillatory modulation across and within CA1, PFC, and OB networks plays a key role in temporal evolution of ensemble dynamics for odor-cued decision making.
source: Our results thus suggest that oscillatory modulation across and within CA1, PFC, and OB networks plays a key role in temporal evolution of ensemble dynamics for odor-cued decision making.
evidence: Overall conclusion synthesizing findings.

claim: Encountering a familiar odor stimulus and efficiently utilizing this associative memory for a decision elicits the engagement of the hippocampal-prefrontal network by the beta rhythm.
source: Based on these findings, we speculate that encountering a familiar odor stimulus and efficiently utilizing this associative memory for a decision, rather than respiration or movement preparation (Hermer-Vazquez et al., 2007), elicits the engagement of the hippocampal-prefrontal network by the beta rhythm.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on findings and cited work.

claim: The lack of SWRs during the decision-making period could reflect that memories had been previously consolidated into neocortex during learning.
source: Therefore, the lack of SWRs during the decision-making period could reflect that these memories had been previously consolidated into neocortex during learning, resulting in a shift from largely hippocampal-dependent processing (Igarashi et al., 2014) to processing that is more reliant on hippocampal-cortical dialogue via the beta rhythm.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of SWR absence with citation.

claim: Beta rhythms play a key role in mediating odor-cued decision making, in addition to coordinating entorhinal-hippocampal networks for odor-cued recall.
source: Instead, our results indicate that beta rhythms play a key role in mediating this process, in addition to coordinating entorhinal-hippocampal networks for odor-cued recall, as described previously (Igarashi et al., 2014).
evidence: Interpretation of findings with reference to previous work.

claim: Local olfactory networks may be governed by gamma rhythms for odor processing early in stimulus sampling, before shifting to a beta-dominant network state as downstream regions are engaged.
source: It has been hypothesized that local olfactory networks may be governed by gamma rhythms for odor processing early in stimulus sampling, before shifting to a beta-dominant network state as downstream regions are engaged (Frederick et al., 2016; Martin et al., 2006).
evidence: Hypothesis from cited literature.

claim: Sensory modality-specific rhythms may play a general role in cue-driven mnemonic decision making by coordinating sensory and cognitive areas.
source: We speculate that sensory modality-specific rhythms may play a general role in cue-driven mnemonic decision making by coordinating sensory and cognitive areas, which can be tested in future studies.
evidence: Speculative generalization based on findings.

claim: Choice-selective cells do not respond solely to the perceptual qualities of the odor but instead code the behavioral choice associated with the odor cue.
source: However, we found that these selective cells often exhibited 'opposite' selectivity on incorrect trials compared to correct trials, indicating that these cells do not respond solely to the perceptual qualities of the odor, in which case the response would be similar on all presentations of a particular odor regardless of the trial outcome. Instead, this response suggests coding of the behavioral choice associated with the odor cue, resembling findings from studies of combined cue modalities and cue-context associations (Allen et al., 2016; Ferbinteanu et al., 2011; Fitzgerald et al., 2011; Komorowski et al., 2009; McKenzie et al., 2014; Otto and Eichenbaum, 1992b; Schoenbaum and Eichenbaum, 1995b; Terada et al., 2017).
evidence: Interpretation of selectivity patterns with citations to similar findings.

claim: The CA1-PFC neural response during odor sampling corresponds to the decision in response to the odor-place association.
source: Thus, the CA1-PFC neural response during odor sampling corresponds to the decision in response to the odor-place association.
evidence: Interpretation based on selectivity analysis.

claim: The timing of ensemble odor discrimination preceded choice execution, indicating that the emergence of the neuronal representation can prime the cognitive decision.
source: Overall, the timing of ensemble odor discrimination preceded choice execution, indicating that the emergence of the neuronal representation can prime the cognitive decision.
evidence: Interpretation of PCA and discrimination timing results.

claim: The emergence of neural ensembles that reflect associative memories governing decision making may be indicative of a physiological mechanism for dynamic reactivation of memory engrams upon re-encountering the familiar odor stimuli.
source: This emergence of neural ensembles that reflect associative memories governing decision making may also be indicative of a physiological mechanism for dynamic reactivation of memory engrams upon re-encountering the familiar odor stimuli (DeNardo et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: Speculative interpretation with citations to engram literature.

claim: A more direct relationship between CA1-OB coherence and performance would be observed only during learning, but not when the odor association and task are familiar.
source: Since previous reports suggest that this coherence is linked to the learning process, it is possible that a more direct relationship between coherence strength and performance would be observed only during learning, but not in this case where the odor association and task are familiar.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of null finding with reference to previous work.

claim: Choice-coding ensemble dynamics may evolve in parallel with the increase in CA1-OB beta coherence over learning.
source: Choice-coding ensemble dynamics may evolve in parallel with the increase in CA1-OB beta coherence over learning, similar to what has been reported in the hippocampal-entorhinal circuit (Igarashi et al., 2014).
evidence: Speculative hypothesis with citation.

claim: Beta driven ensembles mediate memory-guided decision making in the hippocampal-prefrontal network, but choice selective activity is then subsequently maintained by theta-driven spatially modulated activity.
source: Thus, beta driven ensembles mediate memory-guided decision making in the hippocampal-prefrontal network, but choice selective activity is then subsequently maintained by theta-driven spatially modulated activity, similar to reports in spatial working memory tasks (Taxidis et al., 2020).
evidence: Interpretation of spatial decoding results with citation.

claim: Beta and RR coordinate the network cooperatively during odor-cued decision making.
source: This joint modulation of the underlying cell populations, along with our finding of strong cross-frequency coupling between the two rhythms, leads us to the interpretation that beta and RR coordinate the network cooperatively during odor-cued decision making.
evidence: Interpretation based on phase-locking and coupling analyses.

claim: RR could be the dominant modulator coordinating the sensory element of the task, while beta coordination is key for employing the sensory cued association to make a decision.
source: This interpretation is further supported by our results from un-cued air sessions, which did not involve memory-guided behavior, in which we found a reduction in beta coherence in the network but no change in RR coherence. This suggests that the sensory component of this process is maintained as the animal continues sniffing even in the absence of an explicit cue, whereas beta coordination is only engaged when a familiar cue is utilized for a decision.
evidence: Interpretation based on comparison between odor and air sessions.

claim: Entrainment of interneurons to the network-wide beta rhythm is linked to task performance.
source: The higher beta phase modulation of CA1 interneurons also suggests that entrainment of interneurons to the network-wide beta rhythm is linked to task performance.
evidence: Interpretation of interneuron phase-locking results.

claim: Rhythmic modulation of interneurons, possibly through a common input to the CA1-PFC network, can potentially play a key role in temporally organizing ensemble responses to enable processing of odor-cued associations for translation to decisions.
source: Since interneurons have a pre-dominant effect on local network activity, rhythmic modulation of interneurons, possibly through a common input to the CA1-PFC network, can potentially play a key role in temporally organizing ensemble responses to enable processing of odor-cued associations for translation to decisions. (Andrianova et al., 2021; Dolleman-van der Weel et al., 2019; Schlecht et al., 2022; Varela et al., 2014).
evidence: Interpretation with citations to supporting literature.

claim: Beta oscillations may play a role in establishing communication and organization of activity in sensory and cognitive networks enabling decisions based on cued associations.
source: Beta oscillations may thus lay a role in establishing communication and organization of activity in sensory and cognitive networks enabling decisions based on cued associations.
evidence: General interpretation of findings.

claim: Oscillatory phase-modulation may be indicative of a general network state that enables coordination.
source: This oscillatory phase-modulation may be indicative of a general network state that enables coordination.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of phase-modulation findings.
